_comment: Guided tour for accurate-FRET calibration. Targets are real view-spec attrs and real toolbar actions; the steps that act wait for the user to press the button. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: What calibration buys you
steps.text:
A raw FRET histogram is a fact about your microscope. Four factors — α, δ, γ, β — remove what the optics and the dyes put into the counts, and only then is an efficiency a fact about your molecule, comparable with a value measured somewhere else.

A multi-laboratory benchmark showed these systematics, not counting statistics, are what makes FRET values disagree between labs. Ten steps.

steps.title: Point it at bursts
steps.text: The tool calibrates from the bursts you already have — a burst folder from the burst-analysis pipeline, with the per-burst photon counts in it. Nothing is re-searched here.

steps.title: Say which column is which channel
steps.text:
Everything below depends on these three being right, and a swap is silent: the arithmetic still runs and produces a confident, wrong calibration.

IDD is donor emission under donor excitation, IDA is acceptor emission under donor excitation — the FRET signal — and IAA is the acceptor under its own laser, which is what makes stoichiometry measurable at all.

steps.title: Background comes off first
steps.text: Every corrected count is I − Bg, so the background enters before the factors do. An error here shifts the dim bursts and leaves the bright ones alone — indistinguishable, by eye, from a second population.

steps.title: The optics are a prior, not a guess
steps.text:
γ, α and δ are not free parameters: they follow from the excitation and emission probabilities of your light path. Select a saved one and those become Gaussian priors.

The value of that is what happens when the data is uninformative — a file with no donor-only bursts cannot identify α. With a prior it keeps the optical value and the optical uncertainty, instead of a fitted number that looks equally confident and is an illusion.

steps.title: Two routes to γ, and they need different samples
steps.text:
The E–S route fits 1/S = Ω + Σ·E across sub-populations, so it needs at least two populations of different efficiency. A single-species sample cannot give it a slope.

The lifetime route needs only one population, because the donor lifetime carries the efficiency independently of any photon-counting factor. Pick by what your sample has, not by preference.

steps.title: Now calibrate
steps.text:
It fits a mixture to the stoichiometry and labels every burst donor-only, acceptor-only or doubly labelled — no hand-drawn gates, so nobody has to defend where a box was put. α comes from the donor-only bursts, δ from the acceptor-only ones, γ and β from the doubly labelled.

Then it repeats, because the classification depends on the factors it is looking for. Two or three passes is normal.

steps.title: Read the factors — and their error bars
steps.text:
The uncertainties are not decoration. They propagate into every efficiency and every distance you report:

∂E/∂γ = −E(1−E)/γ, and σ_R/R grows as 1/(6·E·(1−E)).

That last one is why a distance near R ≈ R₀ is solid and one at either end of the dynamic range is soft, however many bursts you collected.

steps.title: The check that catches a wrong calibration
steps.text:
Look at the E histogram and find the donor-only population. It is the one answer you knew before you started, and after correction it must sit at E ≈ 0.

If it does not, the factors are wrong — not the sample. Nothing else in this window will tell you that.

steps.title: Afterwards
steps.text:
Share in session publishes the calibration so any fit can link its correction parameters to it — one calibration, many datasets. Export CSV writes the per-burst values with the calibration in the header, so the numbers stay traceable to how they were produced.

It all runs headless too: csc accurate-fret --help. The ? button has the formulas and the citation.
